pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You need a new variable inside a function. When do you reach for `:=` and when for `var`? Is there anywhere `:=` simply doesn't work?
expected_points: := is the default inside functions when there is an initial value
var when you want an explicit type or to start from the zero value
:= is not allowed at package level — package-level declarations need var or const

questions.prompt: After `var n int`, `var s string`, `var b bool` — what does each variable hold, and why does Go guarantee an answer at all?
expected_points: 0, "" (empty string), and false; floats start at 0 too
every declared variable starts at its type's zero value — never garbage or undefined
guaranteed starting points make forgotten assignments predictable instead of mysterious

questions.prompt: What does `7 / 2` evaluate to in Go, and how do you get 3.5? Why won't Go make that conversion for you?
expected_points: Go never converts types implicitly; mixing types is a compile error, so every conversion is visible and deliberate

questions.prompt: Your weekday const block mentions `iota` exactly once, yet Monday through Sunday come out 1 to 7. Walk me through how.
expected_points: iota counts from 0 and increases by one on each line of the const block
a line without an expression repeats the previous line's expression with the new iota
so Monday = iota + 1 gives 1, and the bare names that follow give 2 through 7

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `const x = 3` and `const x int = 3`? When does it matter?
expected_points: untyped constants adapt to the context — usable in both int and float64 expressions without conversion
a typed constant is locked to its type like a variable whose value cannot change
it matters the moment the constant meets a value of another type

questions.prompt: You assign a string to an int variable by mistake. When do you find out, and why is that timing a feature?
expected_points: at compile time, before the program runs — that is what statically typed means
the compiler checks every use of every variable against its declared type
whole classes of bugs are caught before any user can hit them, unlike dynamically typed languages surfacing them at runtime
